Latrobe Magnesium accelerates US ambitions with 50ktpa plan

Engel Schmidl4 days agoSeptember 17, 2026
Latrobe Magnesium’s first 1kg magnesium ingot produced from fly ash using a patented hydromet process. Image: Latrobe Magnesium
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:11
Instaread

Latrobe Magnesium (ASX:LMG) has made a significant shift in its commercial strategy, prioritising a 50,000-tonne-per-annum (tpa) magnesium plant in the US as it seeks to capitalise on growing demand for secure non-Chinese supply.

The proposed South Carolina development represents an acceleration of the international expansion plans outlined by LMG earlier this year, when the company envisaged progressing from its Latrobe Valley demonstration facility to a 10,000tpa Australian commercial operation before pursuing a larger overseas plant.

LMG has identified a preferred South Carolina site and is in advanced negotiations over the location, which has infrastructure, port and logistics access suitable for a 50,000tpa plant and potential expansion to 100,000tpa. The company also intends to negotiate additional feedstock arrangements to support a second 50,000tpa train.

Incoming LMG chief executive officer Robert Stein said the US opportunity had emerged from commercial work undertaken by former chief executive officer David Paterson and the broader LMG team over several years.

“The company’s been doing its commercial work in the background to try to make this opportunity a reality,” Stein told Australian Resources & Investment.

That work is beginning to translate into prospective demand. LMG has secured letters of intent covering 32,000tpa, equivalent to 64 per cent of the proposed initial capacity.

These include an in-principle commitment from Metal Exchange for at least 25,000tpa, alongside 5000tpa from Meridian Lightweight Technologies and 2000tpa from Twin City Die Castings.

LMG said North American customer enquiries have reached 110,000tpa, with global enquiries totalling 285,000tpa.

The strategic backdrop is significant. There is currently no operating primary magnesium producer in North America, while 90 per cent of global supply comes from China.

The US Department of Energy has identified magnesium among 13 commodities carrying the highest supply risk, while LMG is responding to a US Defence Industrial Base Consortium request for project proposals covering magnesium.

LMG’s connection with the US critical minerals strategy also predates the South Carolina plan.

In October 2025, LMG was one of seven Australian companies issued a Letter of Interest (LOI) by the Export–Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) as part of more than $US2.2 billion in prospective financing for US-aligned critical minerals projects in Australia under the US–Australia critical minerals framework agreement.

The other companies were Arafura Rare Earths, Northern Minerals, Graphinex, VHM, RZ Resources and Sunrise Energy Metals.

For LMG, that earlier recognition provides context to the South Carolina strategy, with the company moving from potential US-backed critical minerals financing for an Australian project to considering a substantially larger operation within the US.

“The US policy and policy framework is very supportive of us being able to build a project and get a risk-adjusted return,” Stein said.

Building the South Carolina supply chain

LMG’s proposed US operation would use ferronickel slag secured under its binding 20-year memorandum of understanding with Société Le Nickel (SLN), part of Eramet.

LMG said the agreement contains sufficient optionality to increase offtake volumes to meet the feedstock requirements of the 50,000tpa plant over its proposed 30-year economic life.

The material is stockpiled in New Caledonia and would be shipped through the Port of Charleston to the proposed processing plant.

LMG is in advanced negotiations over the logistics arrangements and preferred development site, although the different components of the project remain conditional on one another.

“We’ve had very strong support from the South Carolina government to the point where they’ve provided an incentives package,” Stein said.

The preferred site provides access to the required utilities and infrastructure, while the proposed state incentives comprise cash, in-kind services and tax holidays, subject to conditions. Bechtel has been nominated as LMG’s engineering partner of choice.

The South Carolina development would represent a major scale-up from the company’s demonstration facility in Victoria’s Latrobe Valley, where LMG has been developing its proprietary process to recover magnesium from industrial waste.

Stein said completing the final stage of the pyrometallurgical process remained important to establishing the technology for commercial deployment.

“The company’s got an asset, and the asset is intellectual property,” he said.

“We’re now in a stage where we’re developing the last stage of the pyrometallurgical process and completing that to then be able to produce finished metal down in the Latrobe Valley.”

US funding interest emerges

The larger US development brings a substantially greater funding requirement, but LMG has now received preliminary interest in funding the work needed to advance the project.

The company has received a non-binding Letter of Support (LOS) for a $US15 million equity investment to fund the feasibility study for the proposed 50,000tpa plant.

The investment is intended to be made by a US-based counterparty into LMG’s US project subsidiary rather than the ASX-listed parent.

Importantly, the proposed investment remains conditional. It requires LMG to secure an equivalent $US15 million of financing from a specified confidential US-based entity, as well as further due diligence, approvals and negotiation of terms.

LMG said it would continue negotiations with other parties over funding for the feasibility study, land acquisition and working capital for the US subsidiary.

The development itself is substantially larger. LMG estimates capital expenditure of $US1.1–1.5 billion, with operating costs of $US2600–4000 per tonne.

At a magnesium price range of $US5000–7500 per tonne, against a stated spot price of $US7050 per tonne, LMG estimates an NPV10 of $US1.4–2.7 billion based on its mid-case capital and operating cost assumptions, and an unlevered internal rate of return of 18–26 per cent.

The company has also outlined an indicative funding concept for the 50,000tpa development, while retaining flexibility to optimise the structure as the project progresses.

“The intended funding is basically project-level equity with a US financial institution or government, or a combination of that,” Stein said.

The proposed structure would fund the US subsidiary directly, with LMG intending to retain majority ownership. It could also provide options to realise value from the business over time.

“If we want to monetise that holding, we can list it, we can sell it down, we can sell it down to JVPs, customers, strategic partners,” Stein said.

For investors, the $US15 million LOS provides an early indication of US financial interest at the project level, but it is not a funding commitment. Securing the matching $US15 million financing and satisfying the other conditions remain necessary before the proposed investment can proceed.

US moves to front of the queue

Despite South Carolina emerging as the priority, LMG continues to consider commercial projects in the US, Malaysia and Australia.

“We’ve essentially got three commercial options in the business,” Stein said. “We’ve got a US option, a Malaysian option and an Australian option.”

The company is weighing those opportunities against factors including permitting timelines, jurisdictional risk and investment fundamentals.

“Everything’s pointing to the US being the fastest alternative,” Stein said.

Engineering undertaken for the first commercial plant could subsequently be applied to other developments, making the choice of the US a question of sequencing rather than abandoning the other options.

“It doesn’t mean that Malaysia or Victoria are off,” Stein said. “It just means that, from an order perspective, it’s just a sequencing question.”

Malaysia remains attractive due to its lower energy costs and proximity to Asian markets, while Stein said there could be opportunities for earlier work there to help de-risk subsequent investment.

The Victorian commercial expansion remains dependent on a favourable resolution of the trailing liability scheme for declared mines.

Long-term feedstock security is central to the Australian development case. Existing arrangements may be sufficient for the demonstration plant, but a larger operation intended to run for more than 20 years would require secure feedstock over a corresponding period.

Stein, a Victorian who grew up in Melbourne’s industrial western suburbs before becoming a chemical engineer, remains committed to pursuing an operation in the state.

“I want to see this investment work in Victoria,” he said. “I want to create economic growth and jobs in the state.”

South Carolina, however, currently offers LMG its quickest pathway to commercial scale.

The change substantially raises the company’s immediate ambition. Rather than progressing from demonstration production to a 10,000tpa Victorian operation before pursuing larger international expansion, LMG is prioritising a 50,000tpa US plant with potential to eventually double in size.

For investors, the opportunity comes with significant execution requirements. Prospective customers already cover almost two-thirds of initial capacity, LMG says its existing SLN agreement can accommodate feedstock requirements over the proposed 30-year economic life, and South Carolina has offered an incentives package. The company also enters the process with an existing connection to US critical minerals policy through its 2025 EXIM LOI.

LMG still needs to secure the site and associated commercial arrangements and complete feasibility work, while the $US15 million Letter of Support and proposed matching financing remain conditional.

Beyond the study phase, establishing a funding pathway for a development carrying estimated capital costs of $US1.1–1.5 billion will be a much larger test.

Those milestones will determine whether LMG can translate its Australian-developed magnesium technology and years of US commercial groundwork into a large-scale North American operation.
